projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Thomas Morrison was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Thomas E. Morrison. Mr. Morrison served with the U.S. Army 601st Tank Destroyers Battalion. He was the cannoneer on a half-track. He served in North Africa and Italy and his highest rank was PFC. I'm Tom Swope. We recorded this at Mr. Morrison's home in East Lake, Ohio on July 29, 2001. Mr. Morrison's age at the time of this recording was 83.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When did you go into the service?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: In May of 1942.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Drafted?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Oh, yes. I tried to enlist, but they wouldn't take me. The first place I didn't have enough teeth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Enough teeth?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How is that? How did that work?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: I had four molars at the bottom that had cracked enamel, and they had gone before I knew what the score was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm hmm?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: So, then I got hit in the mouth with a spike ball when I was working in a railroad. So, I lost two teeth there. So, you could only have four teeth missing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: So, when I went in they told me I didn't have enough teeth. So, a year later they drafted me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: {Laughs}. All right. Where did you train?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Fort Bragg. I went in, they asked me, they said they wanted to be sure that I got into something I knew what I was doing. I said, "Well, I would like to go into a railroad battalion, because I had been a railroad pipefitter." So -- and they asked me what hobbies I had, and so, I told them, well, I liked art and photography, and so they questioned me about different things about how much I knew about both of them, and I told them how much I got into, and so, I ended up in Fort Bragg at radio school. And I said, "Well, what the hell am I doing here? I don't know from nothing in radio." And they said they was suppose to put me in something I knew something about. Well, lieutenant said -- one of them said -- "Well, we got plenty of people that can do railroad pipefitting. He said, "Anybody can do that," said, "but, we need some radio operators for artillery divisions." So, I spent the biggest part of the summer in Fort Bragg with a pair of cans on my ears taking CW. So, I went from nothing to taking -- sending and receiving about 12 words a minute, which was about as good as anybody could.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What does CW stand for?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Continued wave. And so, after -- we're suppose to stay there for 12 weeks, but after eight weeks they shipped us off to the First Infantry Division at the Indian Town Gap. We were getting ready to shove off overseas. So, anyhow they -- I told them, I said, "I'm a radio operator." They said, "Okay." They took me down and gave me a sergeant, and he put cams on and I sent to him, and I put the cams on and he sent to me, and I couldn't receive him. I said, "What the hell is it, I can't understand what he's trying. So, I thought, well, maybe this is something different." So, after he said, "You're pretty good all right. He said you need a lot of practice." So, next thing I know I end up as a cannoneer on a 75 millimeter, on a French 75 on a half-track. So, we sailed overseas on a Queen Mary with a First Infantry Division. I don't know if -- if you was ever told about that or not.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The big red one?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Yeah. I mean on the Queen Mary.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, I didn't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Oh, geez, it was all the First Infantry Division plus a complete hospital unit. I don't know what hospital unit it was, and I think it was an MP unit, plus our battalion, and they had everything. They had bunks built everywhere, and our bunks were in the swimming pool on a promenade deck. So, we -- they had these bunks built in, there were five of them, and they were just about 18-inches space in between. You get down to move in, that's the way you stay. You wanted to turn over on your belly, you had to get out and move back in again. So, first we laid our barracks bags and everything on the floor on the bunk, and lieutenant comes through and says, "Get those barracks bags out of the aisle." Said, "What are we going to do with them?" He said, "That's your problem, son, all I'm doing is telling you." So, we took those in with us. We put them, put the barracks bags in and put our foot over the top of it and then moved in, straddled the barracks bags. So, that's the way we traveled over there. But then we had a pretty good deal. We had ammunition detail. We were suppose to supply ammunition to the antiaircraft guns. And all we did was sit around on the deck. So, it was almost like -- like a vacation cruise, but it only took five days. We left on the 3rd of August and we arrived at Clydeside, Scotland on the 5th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This would be 1943?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Forty-two.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Forty-two. Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Yeah. And then from Clydeside we got on railroad cars and they took us to a place called Wisshof (ph) Scotland. Well, we got off there, and it was raining, and we got these helmets on, these were our new helmets. Three or four kids around then when we put them on said, "Blimiest Jerry", and they took off. So, pretty soon we're standing around, and once we hear the pipes -- hear the pipes, here comes a group of Scotties up the line with their -- in their kilties and everything and playing the pipes, and they marched us all the way back to the YMCA barracks where they put us up for the night. And they had a dance for us and everything. And then we moved out from there, and the reason we stopped over there is because we had to change over to the wider rails, and it took us down to Tidworth, Tidworth barracks, Shalabad (ph) at Tidworth Barracks, and they took us down there and unloaded, and that's where we stayed for, I don't know, I guess it was about two months. Let's see, August, September, October, yeah, November we left for North Africa.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Tidworth barracks, is that in southern England?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Yeah. That was in south central England. It wasn't too far from the coast, but then we did a lot of travelling around in our-- and became familiar with our half-tracks, and it was miserable. I hated riding in the back of those things. Rained everyday just about. And one thing that was interesting, we used to pass by the Stonehenges. You know the Stonehenges near Amesbury. Yeah. Well we would pass by and we would see those in the distance. So, one day the captain, I had to -- from welding and burning, I had my glasses were all covered with slag, you know, so, he was worried about that, he said, he said, "Hey, if I give you the day off said would you go into Amesbury and get yourself another pair of glasses?" He said, "You got the money for it?" I said, "Yeah. I think I've got enough for it." So, he said, "All right." He said, "You take off tomorrow and you go into Amesbury and get yourself, get new lenses for you in those glasses." So, that's what I did. I went into Amesbury. And so, jeweler there said, "Yeah, we can fix that." I think it cost me something like -- like seven pounds, which was -- would amount to about $21.00 at that time. And so, then I wandered up into the Amesbury Cathedral. It's a beautiful cathedral there, and while I was there I met a young girl. She's -- she was an organist from Bath, Bath, England, and so, she was headed for Stonehenge. She was going up to see that. I said, "Well, I'll go see that too." So, after I caught the bus and rode up there, I found out I wouldn't be able to get another bus back until it was too late for me to catch a bus back to Tidworth. So, I just turned right around and come back. I didn't even stop to see the Stonehenges close up. But later on I did, went up to Bath to see her and we stayed overnight in Bath, but it was a dead end because everybody left Bath at night. They had been -- they had been fire bombed by the Germans and burned out. And but a friend of mine, we went up there, we had a pass to go up there for one day and a night. We left England then and went to North Africa. We went in the second wave. We didn't go in the first wave for -- they took the 701 Tank Destroyers. It was the First Armored Division, and they landed at Oran and they wandered all through. They didn't grant hardly any combat at all. I guess they did a few odds and ends, but it didn't amount to anything. But we had it about a month later, and so, we got straightened around and then we took off, and that's when we went up into Tunisia. We went up through the Atlas Mountains.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the name of your unit?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: 601 Tank Destroyers.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: 601 Tank Destroyers. That was a battalion?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Yeah. It was a battalion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were attached to various divisions?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: We were attached to the First Infantry Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The whole time? The whole time?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: At that time we were. Then when we went up into Tunisia, they -- the first action we saw we pulled in on a beautiful morning. We were all spread out there and they told us, well, dig foxholes. So we dug about a spot about maybe six inches deep and big enough to lay in, and here come an Italian plane down through there strafing. He killed a company clerk at headquarters. After that, that's why everybody had a 6-foot foxholey. He went down fast. And then on top of that, here come two British planes through, and our 50 caliber antiaircraft knocked one of those down and the guy landed. It didn't hurt him. He landed. He come over -- But then they took the A Company away from the rest of the battalion and they sent us off to Oran, Naktar (ph), and they told us that we were suppose to be attached to the French, Free French, French unit. So, we got up there into the hills of Tunisia, and it was snowing like a son of a gun. Christmas Eve, and it was snowing. It was melting as fast as it snowed, and the water run down, formed in pools, and it was knee deep, and so, they -- next day, Christmas Day, why we were suppose to move up and go into combat alongside of the French. So, the Second Armored Platoon, they moved out first, and the light platoon they moved out first, and we followed up. And Christmas night we pulled down and on the day after Christmas we moved up into a place called -- alongside of Pishon. And it was the French had a German paratroop outfit, they had them on a cliff. They were dug into this sand stuff cliff, and that was our first action. We fired on those cliffs and we kept blasting them out. After blasting all day, they were still in there; and when it got dark, towards evening why here come these Arabs, we called them gooms (ph), but they were -- I don't know. They had a name. They had a name for it. We mispronounced it. We called them gooms, but they were a different name, and but anyhow, all they did was they had long rifles and they laid their rifles up against the rock, took off their robes and turned them around, and they were brown ordinarily, but they turned them around and they were gray striped, and they disappeared into the rocks. And pretty soon we heard those Germans' yelling, "comrad, comrad," and they come running out, they wanted to give up, but these gooms, they wouldn't hear of it. They went in there and carved them up with their knives, cut their ears off, strung them around their neck. But and that night we moved back and we were suppose to get a Christmas dinner. Well it was a miserable thing. It was all cold, and but we got it anyhow. But then that was probably the last real cooked meal we got for two months. And we moved back into an engine to a palm grove, and we sit there for about a week or so, and then they moved us up and we made a try where the French were trying to get through a pass that -- the Germans had an airport Carowan (ph). It was just on the other side of the mountains, and we were trying to get through this pass, and so, they figured they would use us as tanks. Well, when -- our captain had gotten killed at the first day, so, but there was an inspector from -- it was a major, Major Cushman (ph) from -- from -- from the -- the headquarters of combat. What do you call it? It's -- They call it that because of the shape of the building.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, Pentagon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Pentagon, yeah. Cushman came from the Pentagon, and they, this French general made him take over our platoon, and our platoon did have a lieutenant, it was Lieutenant Marcus, he was from -- I don't know whether you heard of the Marcus Lehmann?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: He was one of the Marcus, part of the Marcus. But anyhow, they thought he was too green to be in charge of a combat outfit. So, they put the major in charge, and anyhow the French lieutenant wanted us to move in and go in and with the tanks with the infantry to take this pass, and he refused to do it. He said this wasn't for that sort of combat. So, the general told him he was up for court martial. So, they sent him back to Washington. They called him back to Washington. So, while he was gone they -- they called in and they sent four light tanks from the First Armored. So, they went in and we followed up with them, and they went in ahead of us and we followed up, and all the way through when the machine guns were firing at us we could hear ripping off the side of our half-track, but they was only 30-30S, and we turn around and come back and two of the tanks got stuck up in there because they had tank traps all through there, but anyhow we came back out. One of our tracks got left there and one of our sergeants went in and he, he and one of the sergeants got broken back to private, they went in and brought our half-track out, and the sergeant he got all kinds of decorations that -- Dick Hammond, was a sergeant got broke down to private, he didn't even get a thank you. Dick was a good guy. He and I were close friends. And so, then after -- after that we pulled back and then the rest of A Company they made some contacts somewhere else, and they had taken a bunch of Italian prisoners plus a few Germans, and so, they come back and they joined up with us, and we moved to Au Celsha (ph), that was a French Bastille up in the hills, the French foreign Legion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm hmm?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: And so, they told us that there was one -- Oh, I was going to tell you about we moved down to Carowan (ph) and we fired on the German bivouac area down there, and the French infantry deserted us, left us there, and the next morning we were all alone. We tried to get out. We found out that the French Infantry had also deserted their own artillery, and we got back here, they were, the artillery were buried in their guns in the sand so the Germans wouldn't get them and they were taking off on foot. So, we pulled out. We pulled up onto a plateau overlooking Carowan. We sat up there for a week, and during that time we saw more of our aircraft get shot down. Germans had air superiority. And after we had been there a week, we dug out gun emplacements up on the hill looking down on Carowan. So on Sunday night they -- Sunday afternoon they pulled through two guns up there and they fired. I guess they saw German big shots moving in and going into church and one of the houses there. So, they got permission from the French to fire on the church and the houses. So, that's what they did. They fired about five rounds into this church and five rounds into the houses, and then they moved back into the olive trees. And so, that night we sat there on the alert and were ready to move out, get out of there, one way or the other. So, they shot up a flare, the Germans shot up a flare, they call it a nine-star flare. Made it seem like daylight. They moved out, moved out, went back through there, back to -- back to the mountains. We must have done a lot of damage. In fact we heard later on that we had killed and maimed several of their big shot officers. And the next day, why we -- we went down and checked. We found out that it was all deserted so we moved out, went back to our original bivouac, and that's when the rest of the -- rest of the company moved in with us. And then we went up to Au Celsha, and from Au Celsha we moved up and we set up on a hill overlooking this valley and it was just my platoon sat on this hill overlooking the valley. The other platoon moved around and took it from the other side. And so, we sat around there, nothing doing all day. Recon company, they went up and down the road and they didn't see anything. So, we're sitting there playing cards and somebody said, "Enemy tank, enemy tank approaching," and sure enough here come a big old Mark VIII Panzer down the road, and they fired on our -- on our CQ, CP, but so, we all fired back at it. And our shells bounced off of it like as if they were pea shooters. It was -- it was those Mark VIII's, I guess they had about four foot of cement on the front plus another 16 inches of steel on both sides of that concrete. We would fire out, just back down, and it fired -- fired a flare up, and a flare come up from each side of the valley. Gee, every tree in the valley turned into a tank, and they started firing at us with these, they were firing these 88s. You would look out there, you would see there would be a shell go by you and then you kind of see a flash out there and you go, oh, here comes another, but that was the flash from the one that passed you, that's how fast. I mean just a blue flash. Anyhow we turned around and pulled back because they had us on the side of the hill. So, we turned around and we pulled back about a quarter of a mile and we sat back there and we could hear these German tanks coming in around us, you know, and so, we didn't know what was happening with the other platoon. So, we sat back there and they started, the artillery started falling in all around us, so and then we moved back about another three-quarters of a mile to the -- to our headquarters, our headquarters, to where our headquarters was, and we tried to get the First Sergeant to come up with some ideas, but he was worse off than we were. So, anyhow we sat there, we sent recons up ahead to check it out, and they said there was something coming down the road. So we pulled out and lined up ready to fire, and what it was, we couldn't tell what it was. We were afraid to fire, afraid it was one of the other platoons. So, we turned around and pulled all the way back to Au Celsha, and we sat up there. It was a British yak yak outfit up there and they had pom pom guns, and boom boom, but so, we all lined up along in front of Au Celsha and the pom pom guns and we're sitting there and here comes Lieutenant Miner and part of the other platoon, and we, the way it was, he said, "We were up there fighting Germans. That's what we're here for. What are you guys doing back here?" That was bullshit because he spent the whole time trying to get out of there and my buddy got a silver star for bringing them out. They lost a lot of the guys there that day. A lot of them were captured. And we didn't lose anybody in our outfit. Anyhow he said, "Come on," he said, "we got to go back up. French Foreign Legion have a whole brigade up there. They're trapped." So, they go up and break them loose. So, we went back up and it was dark and we went back up and they set us up at the bottom of the hill, and we could see the machine guns. The machine guns were searching out the French brigade. And we saw the French brigade, they pulled out and they pulled through us and we fired on those machine guns. The machine guns were on the tanks, and we fired on them, and then they swung around and they started firing on us. First they fired over our heads and then they lowered -- fired down and fired in front, raised us up, and Dick Hammond was driving our truck at the time. He said, "That's close enough." So, we turned around and pulled back, and after we pulled back, why we pulled on back and then we -- we pulled back and about a mile I guess, and we stayed up for the night, and anyway they give us an hour sleep. I know I sat down and fell asleep. Man, that was the prettiest hour of my life. I couldn't believe it that it was time to wake up already. But anyhow that day B Company and part of the First Armored moved up, and they moved in and First Armored Infantry they moved in and they got hit and they came out and then First Armored moved in with the B Company and B Company pulled out. We pulled in behind. I don't know why B Company's captain he was -- I don't know, he just never could stay on the line very long. So, we pulled in behind them, and that's when we saw the -- our -- we had gas-fired tanks, you know, all it took was one hit to the carburetor and they were finished. So, two of them got knocked out, and as they came back through us, why, the captain said, "Hey, you guys want to come aboard and ride with us?" and the captain said, "Hell no, he said, you're nothing but paper armored bastards, all you're good for is drawing fire." So, anyhow we stayed out there and we just sat there. We didn't see anything to shoot at. So, the other three-- the other three guns they fired, shot down cactus all over the place. I don't know. There wasn't anything there. I don't know what they were shooting at. So, Dick Hammond -- somebody is shooting at us though, it was coming over our head -- Dick Hammond, he was our driver, he said, "I think saw something up there." He came back and told the gunner, he said, "Level on that Arab house out there." So, John tried to -- he said, "I can't even see it." So, Dick got up there and he tried to look through the site. He couldn't see it either. So, he got -- he got them to -- he just looked down the barrel of a gun and got them to line it up. We fired and we hit the corner of that Arab house, and here was that gun, that whole crew was sitting underneath of it. And a concussion killed all four of them. And we didn't know it though until we moved up about two days later. Anyhow, we stayed there and we moved up a couple of days and finally they sent C Company up and they took over and we moved back to around Pishon, that area, and I can't remember much about what we did around that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You say there was a three-man crew on a half-track?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Yeah. Three. There was a gunner and number one man and number two man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: My job was -- was first place was just putting the shells into the gun, and the number two-man fired it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And the other drove?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: And of course we had a driver and we had a corporal who was in charge of it that was -- Anyhow after that, we moved to -- we sat around for awhile and then we heard that they -- that they were ran into some trouble. We were stretched out over that whole area there and we had 34th Division was sitting at Fondouk. First Infantry Division was up at Maches El Abab (ph) and First Armory Division, they were spotted here and there, and the -- you couldn't -- you couldn't move on the road because of the Germans had air superiority and as soon as anything hit the roads, why the German planes come down and knocked them out, and so, what happened was the tanks of the First Armored Division was running out of gas up there and we had no way of getting gas to them because we were trying to bring a gag down the road where the German tanks and German planes would knock them out. So, they were in trouble, and German tanks were breaking through the infantry and knocking out tanks, and, so, they called us back into action. So, we moved out towards Faid, moved towards Faid Pass, and that's when we went through -- we went through Sbeitla and went up through the desert up to Faid Pass, and Faid Pass why there was a -- a lot of stragglers came through from where there was another tank destroyer out there got pretty badly mauled, and they were coming back through, and the armored infantry, First Armored Infantry, they were coming through, they were walking and getting through any way they could. And so, the Germans were moving down on from -- they broke through -- broke through at Carowan. 34th Division, anyhow they -- the tanks moved through the 34th Division and they came up through Faid Pass and they came around, they come around through El Guettar. So, there was -- they tell me it was 300 tanks. I don't know whether there was or not, but I know there was a hell of a lot of them come up there because we moved up. The radio operator said there is 50 tanks moving in. And, so, we got up there and we pulled into Faid Pass and that's when our colonel turned us around and brought us back and they set us up. They sent B Company up. They had eight guns and they set them up and they moved us back and set us up. That's when we spent the -- spent the night, that's why we spent the night there, and we were -- we pulled down into a circle and we spent the night there, and that's when -- that's where our own planes come by and strafed us and killed two of our men, and our own antiaircraft shot one of our men off the -- but we pulled down into this area and the next day, and our own artillery was shooting at us, and so, they had a -- when the Germans saw that it was our own artillery that was shooting at us, they figured we were Germans so they didn't shoot at us anymore, but they, after that, they said it worked out where we were and artillery stopped shooting at us, and then we pulled out onto the desert, and like I say B Company lined up ahead of us and then we lined up back of B Company and we looked out there and we saw all of these tanks moving down on us, and B Company they didn't even fire a round, they just turn around and took off. They were suppose to fire four rounds and then move through us, and we were suppose to fire four rounds and then move through them. So, after they pulled through, why we waited until the German tanks got thin in distance and we started firing, and I don't know, we saw something out there, whether it was a truck or what it was, it burst into flame, but we didn't get any credit for tanks, so, evidently it was just a truck. And so, then we all turned around and came back through, and as we came back -- back we saw these tanks sitting there and we thought, uh oh, that's it, we've been surrounded, the Germans have got us, and then we found out that they was part of the Second Armored Division that moved up to help us out. And it was about 50 of our tanks. So, we pulled up. They thought we were Germans. They were going to let us have it until our colonel moved through and told them not to, that was his men. Then we pulled back from there and we set for a long time along the road, and we had to decide what to do, and B Company, they went on through. They just kept right on going. So, we pulled back and pulled back into an olive orchard and sat there for a long time. So, then, well, they told us we had to move out. So, we moved on out from there, and pulled all the way up almost to Kasserine, and there was a place there where crossroads came down from Tilep. Tilep was the airport, and Germans had dropped paratroopers at the airport and taken over, and I know they had gone through our outfit looking for pilots trying to find somebody to fly planes out of Tilep. We had one guy there, he had been one of our drivers. He had been a pilot and he took off with them. And we set there at this crossroads and we were guarding that and during the night tanks came through and the next morning I guess we were the last ones to come through and I was sleeping. I woke up and I looked and I thought, gees, I wonder what that is and I looked over and picked it up, it was a coin, it was all black. I looked around here and I see three or four more coins and a leather purse, like rotten finger bones. So, I picked up the coins and I got about five of them I guess and I put them in my pocket and the next day why I was over there polishing them up trying to see what they were and the other guys in the outfit said, "Where did you get those?" and I told them. So, I give each one of them to one of them and I kept the one I had. And so, I don't know what they did with theirs, but I polished mine up pretty good, but I never could tell what it was. And so, we moved back through Kasserine, moved on back, and on the other side of Tilep there was a mammoth ammunition dump that must have covered five miles all over. And so, they moved us back and we sat there for about an hour and then they called us up and they sent my platoon up to the -- they sent us up -- up -- way up around and into one of the -- one of the valleys that was north of Tilep and led into the valley that led into the -- led into Tilep, and they said German tanks moved up there, and so, we were -- we were placed in with that British yeomanry outfit, British -- It's called Derbyshire Yeomanry. It was a famous outfit. They were known pretty well by the Germans, and all the Germans gave them a good word. All they had was a little -- little I don't think they were three-wheeled carts and they had like a machine gun on the front. It was only -- It wasn't any bigger than a 30 caliber, and anyhow they go out and tease these Germans, you know, pull down, tease the Germans and call back by radio. I couldn't even understand them. These are Limies, hard to understand anyhow, and I hear them talking and they talk real funny, and the guy on the other end, he was taking notes, and I would say, "What did he say?" He told me. "How do you understand that?" "It's easy. Just listen." But anyhow they get up there and they would pull in -- pull in close to these German tanks and German tanks you would sort of line up on them and they would pull over and they couldn't move 'em so much, the Germans couldn't hit them, and then the Germans didn't fire, they would take that little gun and shoot in there and just aggravate them until the Germans fired back. But anyhow, we set up there, and I developed a damn bad case of diarrhea. It was, what do they call it, amoebic dysentery. Man I was so sick. Man I was so weak I couldn't stand up. Finally there was a British colonel came out and he found out that I had diarrhea so he sent me back to the hospital. After I left, I guess that was the end of it. Everything was over by that time. The Germans had moved out. And anyhow I went to the hospital and I was in the hospital for two weeks and they couldn't get it stopped. They were worried, you know, because they thought the Germans had been out spreading poison, you know. And I slept most of the time because I was so weak. So, they finally got me straightened out. They give me shots of sulfadiazine in the arm. It was the first time they had tried that. It was an experimental thing, and that worked. And, so, then they sent me back to the outfit, and cripes they sent me all the way back to Second -- Second Armored Division, headquarters of the Second Armored Division. And I got there. Here was -- I didn't know Patton had a brother. This guy, this is Colonel Patton. He was a commander of headquarters of the Second Armored Division. And so, when I went there he said, "Well, stay with me." He said, "That's okay." He said, "I don't have any privates. They took all of my privates away from me and sent them up front. So, I need a private to boss around." He said, "All of these are four stripers I got up here." It was all sergeants with lozenges and up and down stripes. So, they anyhow then they sent me down to the tank destroyer pool they called it. And so, I was -- so, while I was there my colonel came out then and he picked me up and took me back to headquarters and from there I got a ride into A company. END OF SIDE ONE, DISK ONE; BEGIN SIDE TWO, DISK ONE For that ride, the guy that took me, took me back, took me from headquarters back to A Company, he took a shortcut, you know, and I told him I said, "Hey, these are Italians." I said, "That's an Italian uniform." He said, "Nah," he said, "Those are French." So, we went through, and here is these guys standing with their mess kits, and we drove through, and these guys are watching us go by, and I said, "Those are Italians," and he said, "No, those are French." So, we got through, they didn't stop us. We went on through and got back to A company, and I told them, I said, "Hey, that guy took us through an Italian bivouac area." They said, "Where was that?" And I told them, and they said, "Yeah, that was probably Italian." Said, "There is no French out there." Said, "That's all Italian over there." Anyhow, we got to -- We sat around there for about a month, and then I did everything possible trying to get my strength back. I dug sump holes and covered them up and did everything. And then they finally, they put me on a different -- on a brand new M3 with a Sergeant Swartz, and I had different -- I was still the number two man loading a gun. And so anyhow this is a good outfit. The other outfit I had to do all the work. In this outfit why I had a guy by the name of Cordana (ph) and I called him Corky. The other guy was Charlie Hurd. And so, we got along good together. It rained most of the time. We moved up together. So, when we moved into, over towards El Guettar, we didn't have much to do. The Italians -- It was all Italians. "Hey Paisan, hey comrad." They came down, pulled into one place where the Italians were dug in on a sand dune, and this one guy come down, "Hey, paisan, paisan," and he said, he showed us he wanted to give up. So, here come the officer down the hill and he had two guys carrying his suitcases and he was carrying a bottle of wine, and he came down and he offered the bottle of wine to our captain, and of course, the Sergeant Hicooley, he took a shot and said it was anisette wine. First time he ever tasted it and so anyhow it must have been about three or 400 Italians coming down off of the hill, gave up. And so, then we sat there for awhile and then we moved up. And we moved up into the desert there just before the sand dunes, and so, then, the Germans threw a what they call a -- what do you call that an -- it's where they -- they -- they -- they -- they dive bombed us first. They sent waves of dive bombers down, and they came down and dive bombed us. And then they, after that then they sent tanks. So, after they dive bombed us and our lieutenant, Lieutenant Marcus, he got hit in the arm, and our radio operator got killed, and the -- the other radio operator, he was a corporal, he lost his arm. And so, then we got in another -- another officer, he only lasted one day and they took him out of there because he broke radio silence. He told everybody they had to stay on the guns, everybody stay on the guns, and he wasn't suppose to break radio silence. So, they took him out, and so, Pete Hicooley got Lieutenant Miner, who we all liked Lieutenant Miner, he knew what he was doing. So, Lieutenant Miner came down, and we took the guns off of the back of the half-tracks and off of the back of the trucks and we took gun emplacements. So, when -- we never had to use those because that night we moved on up and we dug in on the -- in the front of the sand dunes. We worked all night digging in, and I know I -- I was so exhausted, I didn't have anything to eat, and they come up with a can of corned beef, and so we opened that up and that's what I ate, and I went over and laid down and fell asleep and just starting to break dawn and somebody come over and kicked me and said, "Hey, tanks are coming," and about that time, bam, one of them shot through there. So, I jumped up and jumped on the back of the half-track and we started shooting back, and so, it was real foggy out there, and on top of that the Germans were throwing down smoke grenades, and the tanks kept moving out. One of them pulled all the way over and he got tangled up in a salt marsh, and he was stuck out there, and but the artillery, Lieutenant Miner, they had Lieutenant Miner calling the artillery shots because the line to the artillery up in front, Company B and C had moved over onto the flats and they were annihilated from us. They just had to do the best they could. And the artillery was over there too, and they spiked their guns and walked out on foot. But we had a couple of the 105's back of us, howitzers, and Lieutenant Miner called those artillery and on the tanks were coming up and we knocked out about 35 tanks, and then the infantry decided to move up. Well, I don't know what it was -- you say you saw Patton and his artillery and his infantry come moving up and come walking up, and Miner called down a high burst artillery on them and he wiped them out. We shot into them, too. We were shooting delayed action and it would hit the sand and it would bounce in the air and explode. So, they did a lot of damage, too. But anyhow, we finally we run out of -- we run out of ammunition. So, they told us to come back. So, we pulled back and the driver already, he got out, he wouldn't stay there, and so, our Sergeant Swartz, the tank was, the motor was running, so, Swartzy got out and he came up to us from the maintenance pool, so, he pulled back and he pulled back over the sand dune and he parked us down in below the sand dune, and after that, why, he, Swartz, Sergeant Swartz, he had me clean out the ammunition. We had these slits in the floor of the half-track that we kept ammunition. So, it was full of sand because these, all of these shells bursting around us, they were throwing sand on us.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm hmm?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: So, I had to clean all of that sand out, and then they brought ammunition up to us, and so, he handed the ammunition to me, and I loaded the -- all the things up with ammunition. I brought some gasoline over and I loaded the gas tanks. They were 30-gallon tanks. We had 60 gallons there. So, I loaded the tanks and then I -- after that I got out and I dug a foxhole. Swartz said, dig that big enough for me too. So, I dug a big long trench for both of us. And after that I got down. And we used to heat water for coffee by -- we would take the sea ration can and we would fill it half full of sand and then pour a couple of ounces of gasoline in there and we would light it and set the -- we would usually we punch holes in the side so it would get air, and we would set the canteen cup on top of it with water. So, I made myself a cup of coffee and I was eating, had some sea rations, and so, they said, "All right, mount up we're going back up again." So, I went over with the -- I had my canteen and cup of coffee and I crawled up and I was going to get in the back of the half-track and the guys asked me, "Where did you get the coffee?" I said, "Well, I got a fire going, hand me a canteen cup of water and I'll get it for you." So, I took their canteen cup and took it down, crawled down in the hole and set it on the fire, and I crawled back out and I was setting next to the half-track drinking my coffee and I heard this shell coming in, and I kind of hunched down. When it hit, it threw me into the foxhole, and I knew I got hit in the mouth with something, I didn't know what it was, whether it was my coffee cup or whether it was my helmet. We were completely covered by smoke, and I crawled out of the -- up out of the ditch, and I heard somebody say, "Two guys in that half-track yet." And so I run back and I tried to get in. I couldn't get in. It was blazing. What had happened, that shell had landed in the right hand gas tank, it was a model 155. Two guys, they didn't know what hit them. So, anyhow, I run back around. I didn't know where to go or what to do, and the half-track was burning, and so, I heard the sergeant, he went up to the captain says, "I couldn't, I couldn't get them." He broke down and -- and he was crying. So, they hauled him off to the hospital. I didn't know what to do. I was just walking around there in a daze; and so, I saw some guys outside and I'll go see what they are doing. So I walked across to them. So when I went across, here come a plane down, dive bomber. He was strafing, and he tried to hit the -- tried to hit the radio, the artillery radio observation post, and he missed that. I went on over, and it was -- I was first medic, first medic over there. So, I was standing talking to them and I had to -- I picked up a helmet. I didn't even notice in one of the -- it was a couple of civilians up there, and one of them says, "Hey, you, were you wearing that helmet when you got that?" And I looked at the helmet, the whole side was knocked out of it. So, I must have been sitting on top of the gas tank. And I said, "Well, I guess so. I don't know." And but it wasn't -- it was Charlie -- Charlie Hurd's helmet, and so, the guy they wanted to take my picture with it and they said the picture would be on the front page of Look Magazine. I said, "Oh, no." I said, "I don't want my mother to see that." So, I wouldn't let him take my picture. So, later on I walked on down. They were headed back to -- they were going back to get lunch, and so, I run into a guy I knew, a guy by the name of Cafsa (ph) from headquarters, and I asked him what he was doing up there, and he said, "Where is the front line?" I said, "Well, you go, you look around that bend there," I said, "and you see the front line." I said, "First shell that comes through there hits you, because that's where it is." So, he was driving a three-quarter ton truck, and he said, "What are you doing here?" I told him, "That smoke you see is coming from my half-track. I'm the only one left." So, he said, "Come on, get in. I am suppose to take you back." So, he took me, and a few other guys was sitting around there, took us back to headquarters. I wound up back there, and my buddy who was an ammunition corporal, he got me lunch and I fell asleep in that, so, he put me into his -- he had a hammock stretched out there, and you get in, he said get in there. So I crawled in there and I went to sleep. And during the night, why, Lieutenant Moder(ph) come by and knocked me out of it, said there were some air raids and get into a hole. He run down into a sump hole. So I found a hole there and I crawled in and I went to sleep again, and come daybreak, they were dropping these little bombs, you know, what do you call them, anyhows, they were dropping these personnel bombs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm hmm.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: And, so, next day I run into Mike Dragon (ph) and a few others from our outfit and they said that they were waiting to get assigned to something. And I don't know what -- I don't know really how later on they took me back to A Company and I asked them where A Company was and I saw our A Company mess sergeant. He said, "Hang up your hat," he said, "you're A Company." And then later on, why, there was a few guys come straggling in, and so, then we went from that, then we wandered back, and then Lieutenant Miner and Sergeant Hicooley came back and they sent us -- we moved all the way back to Tilep. We were staying next to Tilep Airport, and then from there I was assigned to a -- to another -- another gun crew, and then we -- we moved up after that. I don't remember. We -- we sat around and didn't do much of anything, but then we went back around by way of Oslata (ph). Not -- not Oslata, but oh, anyhow, we went back through Faid Pass. I know we -- we were staying at Faid Pass and I was on guard that one night. Each night we would get into a -- form a circle, and I was pulling guard and I heard this damn noise. I thought, what the hell is that? And we had heard the French talk about these mountain lions up in that area, and so, after I got off of guard duty I told the guy that relieved me, I said, "Be careful," I said, "there is something out there making a hell of a noise." So, he went out. Pretty soon he come running back. He said, "What is that?" I said, "Well, I don't know," I said, "but maybe it was a mountain lion." So, I was trying to go to sleep. I was wanting to go to sleep. He said, "Don't go to sleep and leave me here all alone." I said, "Well," I said, "I got to get some sleep too." I said, "You had your sleep." And so, we sat around there until daylight. Here what it was was an Arab had pulled up there and set his tent up at night and he had a camel and a mule and that camel -- and a donkey and that donkey would go hee haw hee haw and that damn camel, the camel go rar, rar (ph), and the two of them together they made such -- such a hell of a racket that it scared the hell out of us. So, Lieutenent Moder he made them get up and move on. So, they moved out. And then each day we would move up about a mile and dig in. I wore blisters on my blisters digging those half-tracks in, and one day we were sitting out there, and I see something moving out in the distance out in the desert and Lieutenent Moder says, "Enemy, definitely the enemy, it's too big for anything else." So, we set our guns up and followed it, and come up here was a Salvation Army truck. And we found out that the 8th Army had already moved past. They had moved back two days before. So, then we pulled back and then we moved on around. We moved into -- down -- and moved down -- I can't think of the name of the valley we moved into. Anyhow, that's where we got -- we got our new -- we got our new Italian commander, Colonel Tardi (ph). He was just a major then. But he moved in. I can't think of the name of the valley. Anyhow, we stayed at that and we moved up, followed up on the First Armored Division and First Infantry, and then I got an attack of appendicitis and they took me back -- back to the hospital, and when I got there the pain was gone and this doctor said, "Oh, no," he said, "you're not going to pull that on me." He said, "Get out of this bed." He said, "You just want to get out of the front lines." He said, "I need -- I need bedpan pushers and ward boys." He said, "You're a ward boy now." So, that's what I was doing. I went over and this nurse had me working around there collecting towels and giving baths, and these guys were all up on ropes and helpless. And so, I come by with an armload of wet towels and she had spilled her alcohol all over her and when she went to light her alcohol burner, she set the thing on fire. So, I went over and threw these wet towels on and put it out. She took off on a run. And so, this one captain said, "Hey," he said, "you get a commendation for that." I said, "Nah, I don't want no commendation." He said, "Yeah, but this tent would have caught on fire." I said, "No, it wouldn't." I said, "It's been sprayed." I said, "These tents have all been sprayed." I said, "After Barnum and Bailey had their tents burn out, they made it a point that all tents had to be sprayed." So, I said, "It wouldn't have burned. Otherwise when the hot flack hit the tent it would have caught on fire." He said, "Well, you ought to get a commendation anyhow." I said, "No, don't turn it in. It will just make them put a bad mark against the nurse." So, after that, why the North African campaign was over. So, the guys were moving through, my active were moving back through me. So, I picked up with them and we went back and we were -- we had charge of guarding prisoners then. They came back and they rolled off the barbed wire. The prisoners set the wire up themselves. So that's what we did after the African campaign, we sat there and listened to the Germans and Italians sing. That's all I know, gee, we sat there, and we had a trip into Tunis, and then we moved out, moved over into olive orchards back of Naktar and we were -- we got rid of the half-tracks and the -- they got the M10's. We got all new guys in. They all had promotions. They were all sergeants, corporals. We didn't have any. We were still privates.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Ha.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: So, they said, "Well, anywhere you would like to go? We'll try to get you transferred." So, I said, "Well, I would like to be a medic." I said, "At least I know something about medics," because I had a Red Cross certificate from the YMCA on life saving and first aid. So, I went in as a medic then and I went to Italy as a medic, I went. Nothing much -- nothing much exciting happened. But we went -- some of our guys went into Sicily, but they just went over to guard prisoners, but we got a battle star for that. But, I don't know, it was -- it wasn't very much happened in Italy. We just kept moving up and moving up and behind the artillery, and moved all the way up until us and the British come together, so we had to pull back and take another --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your highest rank then, Private?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Private First Class.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: PFC?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: As a medic I got Private First Class. I understand they had me -- they had me up for T5, but it was on record, but I never got paid for it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of any particular buddies that were close to you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Oh, yeah, like I say Dick Hammond, he was close to me, and he was broken down from a sergeant, and at the start of the Battle of Kasserine why they give him his sergeant's ranking back and he had one of the half-tracks, and he got out to see why it was hung up and a shell hit the side of the half-track and I guess it killed him too. But I got pretty close to the two guys that was killed in El Guettar, Cordana and Hurd. I finally went into the hospital to have my appendix taken out, and then we -- while I was in there, why, they told us that, "Well, your outfit is moving out, they are going back to England." They said, "Do you want to go back with them?" And I said, "Yeah." That was only four days after I was operated on. So, they sent me back to my outfit on the fifth day and I come back and, "Christ, how come you're walking so funny?" I said, "I just got my appendix taken out." And the sergeant says, my sergeant says, "Nah, he said, I had mine taken out," he said, "I was in the hospital 30 days, and then I got a 30-day leave of absence." And he said, "I just saw you last Monday." I said, "Yeah, well that's when I went in to have my appendix taken out." And he said, "Well, no, they don't do that." I said, "Well, they did with me." What happened was I was operated on and they gave me a spinal and after they operated on me I asked the colonel, I said, "Was that appendix bad?" He said, "Yeah," and he held it up like that and showed it to me, and he put me back in bed, and I woke up in the morning, and a nurse woke me up and told me, said, "Come on, here is some chicken for you." So, I ate that and I said, "About when can I move off of my back?" She said, "You can move off your back." She said, "You can get up and run around if you want to." I said, "Okay." When she left, I got up and walked around, and I was kind of lightheaded, and I sit down on the side of the bed again and I felt better. I got up and walked around again, and the guy that was next to me, he said, "What happened to you?" I said, "I had my appendix taken out." He said, "That's what I had. I laid here for over two weeks," he said, "I can't even get off of my back." I said, "Well, that's what they told me they did." So, the nurse come back and I was back in bed and she says, "Do you want to get up and dangle your legs on the side of the bed?" and the guy in the bed next to me he said, "Dangle his legs," he said, "he been all over the ward already." He said, "He been walking all around." She said, "He was?" I said, "Yeah, you told me I could." She said, "Oh, I was only kidding." So, then about then they moved me out of that ward then because one of the kids in there that had been rolling a tank of oxygen and the thing exploded and blew his legs off. So, they moved me out of there because he was keeping me awake. I said, "Can't you put his legs up in ropes or something?" And they said, "He doesn't have any legs." So, anyhow they moved me out. And Bob Hope came there while I was there and I asked if I could go out and see him, and the colonel wasn't sure if he would let me go or not, but he got busy doing something else and he didn't tell me no. So, when it come time to take me out, the nurse said, "What did the colonel say?" I said, "Well, he didn't say no." So, they took me out. I would have like to have died, I laughed so hard. And so, like I say, I went back, and the fifth day I was wandering around, and so, in less than a week they made the invasion into Southern Italy, and so, I was suppose to make that, and my doctor said, "No, you better not, said you better wait and make the next wave." So, I went back by the next wave, and anyhow I was -- I was -- we were back in a farmyard there and a -- big, big farmyard, and it was all surrounded by barbed wire entanglement, and there was a dog fight, two German planes and a British plane. British plane got knocked down. And the British plane got knocked down and was coming around and around in a circle, and it came right over our heads right through the trees, and I was backing up and I fell right over this barbed wire entanglement, fell backward. So we went over to see the plane, couldn't get near it because it was burning, and as we were walking back, one of the kids said, "Hey, doc, what, did you get hit?" I said, "No, why?" "Look your bleeding." I look down and I had blood running down. So, I looked and here my appendicitis scar had ripped open.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, boy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: And so, I made a -- being a medic, I made what they call butterflies. I knew what they were. You twist a tape together and put one -- I put three of those across and pulled it together, and I put a fresh bandage on, and a couple of days later why we were walking through a peach orchard, and, oh man, these were beautiful peaches and they were delicious. So, I -- German planes come down strafing and bombing, and so, I saw this -- this doctor, and I asked if he would take a look at this, you know. So, he looked at it and he said, "Yeah." He said, "Yeah, you better go back to the hospital." I said, "Oh, no, I don't want to go back to the hospital." Said, "If I go back there I get sea rations. Here I get peaches." (Laughs). He was eating a peach himself. He said, "Well, it's up to you," he said, "if you want to go back," he said, "but keep an eye on that." He said, "If it starts to smell, you report yourself in." So, it never got bad, and we had peaches and watermelons and fresh tomatoes. And I know he saw me a couple of times, and he said, "You still up here," he said, "don't you ever get a break?" And we went to Anzio, and on Anzio why I got pretty badly shook up because they dropped -- they dropped bombs on us at night, dropped personnel bombs, and I had to take one guy to the hospital because he got hit in the side of the head with a hunk of shrapnel from a personnel bomb. And the next day I didn't get any sleep, and so, I was sitting in a foxhole, I was doing some paperwork, and a shell came in right past my head and exploded behind me. It was so close I could smell the cordite on the shell, and it exploded behind me. And so I went over, and here the cook got hit right in the head. That's where the shell exploded, and one of the -- of the -- the one guy, one of the guys got a piece of shrapnel in his leg. Well, I couldn't do anything with that. And the other guy had twisted around and broke his leg, and his leg was all twisted like a dishrag. And so, I didn't know what to do, because I didn't have any splints or anything. I tried to find something to make splints out of. So, I called to Sergeant -- I can't think what his name was. Anyhow. I called him and said, "Hey, get on the radio and get ahold of an ambulance and get out here." I said, "I can't handle this by myself." He said, "There is an ambulance right over here." He said, "I just saw it." He said, "I'll go over and get them." So he brought them over and this doctor looked at him and said, "You still here?" I said, "Yeah," I said. But he said, "You don't look too good." I said, "No, I'm pretty tired." And so, anyhow, he took care of the busted leg and he put a -- they had a framework that fit over the -- for a splint, and they put that on, and the other guy, he was taken care of, and this doctor said, "You're suffering from combat fatigue." He said, "You got to go back and get straightened out." So, he sent me back to the hospital, and after I got back there, why they -- they sent me on back to Naples, and in Naples why I saw these guys. I said, gees, come to find out I was the only guy saw any combat. The rest of these guys were gangplank. First time a shell burst near them they went into -- but I got so I wouldn't even take their pills. These pills they were giving out, these sodium amatol, and I didn't want them. It was a pill. So, Salvation Army or Red Cross came through and they were passing out sheets of charcoal pencils and charcoal paper. So, I did sketches of all the guys in there with me. We had them hanging up. This doctor came through and said, "Who did them?" And the guy said, "He did." So, the next day I was on my way back to the outfit, and anyhow, I went back to -- back to my outfit and they sent me back to the section I was in. I was in Naples yet. So, I went back to the one in Naples, and I sat there for about a month and my own doctor, my company doctor, he said, "You had enough of it." He said, "We better send you back again." So, he sent me back, and when they sent me back, why they had me up before this jury of psychiatrics (sic) I guess. This one -- said, he said, "What is with your outfit?" He said, "I have got a dozen guys from your outfit that's gone through here, and said they are all suffering from combat fatigue and psychosis." And I said, "Well, you see too much combat." He said, "What combat?" So I started naming off the battles we had gone through. He said, "Oh, no, nobody in American Army has seen that much combat," and the other colonel said, "Oh, yeah." He said, "I checked it out," and he said, "they have gone through all of that combat." So, then they sent me back to 5th General Dispensary, and because I was a photographer, why they put me in there as an x-ray technician. So, I was an x-ray technician for the dental technician. So, that's what I did for about, I guess about three months, and the colonel come back one day and he said, well, he said the jobs you guys do, you're entitled to a staff sergeant's rating. He said you got a choice, he said, you either go home or you get a staff sergeant's rating. I said, I want to go home. So, I went home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about that reunion with family when you got home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Morrison
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Well, I came -- when I got back to the States, I called my mother. They give me a phone call and I called my mother. And then after -- after they -- I went to Camp Atterbury, Indiana and they got me -- gave me a new outfit and blankets and everything, and these new fangled barracks bags you put on your shoulder instead of those old blue jobs, and -- and I got money and a ticket on the railroad to go home, and I -- I had so much money. I think it was a hundred dollars, I think they give me the first time, and then I -- so I went to -- took a train to -- from Camp Atterbury to Crestline. I had to take a train from there to Masteline or to Canton. I took a train from there to Canton. Canton I got off there and I -- I wandered around Canton for awhile until I got a streetcar home and I met a guy I used to work with. He was a pipefitter, and I said, "Well," I said, "I don't know how I'm going to get from Masteline home," and he said, "Well, take the company bus." I said, "Will they let me ride it?" He said, "Oh, yeah. You can ride it. You're still a company employee as far as they are concerned." So, I rode the Brazilian bus home. And so, when I was downtown I got -- I met a bunch of people at the YMCA that I knew and your crew caller there then by the name of Dick Havering, he had lost a arm. I had taken his job as a caller, and so, he came back and he had my job. So, he took me home, dropped me off, and I came in. My mother was there and my father and my brother and my younger sister and my sister, Agnes, she was there too. I was at home for about two weeks, and then I had to report back to Florida for rest and relaxation, just a couple of days before Christmas. I hadn't been home for Christmas in three years. So, anyhow I had a beautiful time in Florida. Eat, I thought I would get fat because everything was free, you know, Morris's Cafeteria you go in there any time of the day or night, all the fruit you wanted and they had the food all laid out there and eat anytime you wanted. And they had these soda fountains running milkshakes, ice cream sundaes, banana splits, and I ate all day long, I ate and I laid around on the beach and swam. The water was beautiful. And then after I left there I had to go back to Camp Atterbury, or I want to say -- Where did I go? I went to Camp Forrest, Indiana, and they -- from there they discharged me and I went back to Camp Atterbury and from there I went home.
